articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding the blocking and rejecting of transactions and the filing of reports with OFAC. This update aims to provide clearer guidance to U.S. persons and financial institutions on their compliance obligations under various sanctions programs.

The amendments address common inquiries and scenarios encountered in practice, offering detailed explanations on when to block property or reject transactions, as well as the proper procedures for submitting required reports to OFAC. This ongoing refinement of guidance is crucial for maintaining effective sanctions enforcement and ensuring compliance within the financial sector.
The updated FAQs are immediately effective and can be found on the OFAC website, serving as a vital resource for compliance professionals navigating the complexities of U.S. sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Designations, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, and Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations as part of its ongoing efforts to counter illicit activities. Concurrently, OFAC removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea, signaling a recalibration of sanctions policy in these regions.

In addition to the designations and removals, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses. These licenses authorize specific transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, providing carve-outs for certain activities, including wind-down operations and limited safety and environmental transactions involving recently blocked persons or vessels.

The agency also amended existing Frequently Asked Questions to provide further clarity on the scope and application of these new measures, particularly concerning transactions related to the potential sale of Lukoil International GmbH.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Under Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has designated five entities under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) in connection with the theft of trade secrets from U.S. persons.

These designations target entities connected to People's Republic of China national Linwei Ding, who was convicted of stealing Google's trade secrets related to super intelligence (SI) technology. The sanctioned entities include Beijing Qiji Chuangtan Phase I Venture Capital Center Limited Partnership (MiraclePlus RMB Fund I), Beijing Qiji Chuangtan Phase II Venture Capital Center Limited Partnership (MiraclePlus RMB Fund II), and Shanghai Zhisuan Technology Co Ltd (Zhisuan).

Concurrently, OFAC issued PAIPA General License 1, authorizing transactions pursuant to the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations, and PAIPA General License 2, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving certain entities blocked on October 19, 2026.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ for Earthquake Relief
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License (GL 60A) and an updated Frequently Asked Question (FAQ 1263).

This amendment extends the authorization for transactions related to earthquake relief efforts in Venezuela, replacing and superseding the previous GL 60. The extension provides continued flexibility for humanitarian aid and recovery operations in the country.
The updated FAQ reflects the extended authorization period, ensuring that U.S. persons and entities involved in relief efforts have clear guidance on permissible activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-Related and Cuba Designations, Issues New and Amended General Licenses and FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation, intensifying pressure on these regimes.

In conjunction with these actions, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs). These updates aim to provide guidance on permissible transactions and activities in light of the new designations, particularly concerning the Cuba Sanctions Regulations (CSR) and the Cuban Assets Control Regulations (CACR).

The new Cuba sanctions regulations, implemented through a Final Rule in the Federal Register, fully implement Executive Order 14404, 'Imposing Sanctions on Those Responsible for Repression in Cuba and for Threats to United States National Security and Foreign Policy.'

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation.

This action signifies a targeted adjustment in the U.S. sanctions program concerning Venezuela. The delisting notice officially removes the individual from OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) blacklist, ending the associated asset freeze and obstacles for U.S. persons attempting to deal with them.
The removal of Jorge Rodriguez, President of Venezuela's National Assembly, from the SDN list comes amid a broader U.S. push for diplomacy and expansion of energy investment in Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations under its Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism sanctions programs.
These actions target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and terrorist financing networks, aiming to disrupt their operations and financial support structures globally.

The designations underscore the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to combating transnational criminal organizations and terrorist groups that pose a threat to national security and international stability.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement Agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics; Designates International Criminal Court and Issues General Licenses; Removes Burma-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based forwarding and logistics company, for apparent violations of U.S. counter-narcotics sanctions and reporting obligations.

In a significant move, OFAC also designated the International Criminal Court (ICC) as an institution under Executive Order 14203, 'Imposing Sanctions on the International Criminal Court.' This designation follows previous sanctions against individual ICC judges and prosecutors.

Concurrently with the ICC designation, OFAC issued four general licenses authorizing specified transactions involving the court to protect U.S. interests, including a 180-day wind-down authorization. Additionally, OFAC removed a Burma-related designation.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State / Global Sanctions and Export Controls Blog

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued a new Russia-related General License (GL 135).

This general license authorizes certain transactions related to the import of Russian diesel fuel to the U.S. until April 7, 2027. This action comes amidst global energy market dynamics and aims to address potential shortages.

The issuance of this General License follows President Trump's executive order on October 16, 2026, which waived the majority of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs introduced by the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Clyde & Co / The Guardian

articles.headline: EU Imposes New Sanctions on North Korea Over WMD Programs and Russia Ties
body: The Council of the European Union has adopted additional restrictive measures against three individuals and four entities under its autonomous sanctions list on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK).

These designations target those responsible for supporting, promoting, or facilitating activities that contribute to the DPRK's programs related to nuclear weapons, ballistic missiles, or other weapons of mass destruction, as well as for violating and evading United Nations sanctions.
The new listings specifically target activities linked to the growing military and economic cooperation between the DPRK and Russia, underscoring international concerns about their collaboration.
articles.source: Council of the EU / NK PRO

articles.headline: EU Renews Sanctions Against ISIL/Da'esh and Al-Qaeda Until October 2027
body: The Council of the European Union has renewed its autonomous restrictive measures against ISIL/Da'esh and Al-Qaeda, and persons, groups, undertakings, and entities associated with them.

The sanctions regime has been prolonged for another year, until October 31, 2027. The autonomous list currently includes 15 persons and 8 groups, all subject to an asset freeze and, for individuals, a travel ban to the EU.

These measures are complementary to those imposed by the UN Security Council and reaffirm the EU's commitment to countering the ongoing terrorist threat posed by these organizations and their affiliates.

articles.headline: Cuba Accuses U.S. of Threatening Countries Ahead of UN Embargo Vote
body: Cuba has accused the United States of threatening countries with tariffs, visa restrictions, and other retaliatory measures in an effort to influence their votes on an upcoming United Nations resolution calling for an end to the long-running U.S. embargo against the island.

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez stated that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Washington's ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, are personally leading a campaign to pressure UN General Assembly members to vote against the resolution.

The UN General Assembly has historically voted overwhelmingly in favor of non-binding resolutions seeking to end the U.S. economic embargo on Cuba, which has been in place for over six decades and is credited with exacerbating economic hardship on the island.

articles.headline: U.S. Proposes Restrictions on Investments in Sensitive Technology Sectors in Iran and Other Countries
body: The U.S. Treasury Department has proposed new rules that would restrict American investments in sensitive technology sectors in Iran, China, Cuba, North Korea, and Russia.

These proposed rules would require U.S. firms and individuals to notify the Treasury about certain prospective investments in these countries, while outright prohibiting some transactions. Specifically, covered investments in artificial intelligence technologies in the targeted countries would be banned.

This initiative marks the latest expansion of Washington's use of investment controls, alongside export restrictions, to prevent sensitive U.S. technology and capital from supporting potential military capabilities abroad.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
